case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: In a case against Kentucky CHFS social workers, the court held the Fourth Amendment governs a social worker's warrantless in-school interview of a child and requires at least reasonable suspicion of abuse (though that right was not clearly established, so those defendants received qualified immunity), and it affirmed the denial of qualified immunity on the parents' substantive and procedural due-process claims arising from a coerced 'prevention plan' that restricted a mother's unsupervised contact with her children.
key_cases.relevance: It holds that a purportedly voluntary safety or prevention plan is not voluntary where consent was procured by a threat of removal, defeating the agency's Smith v. Williams-Ash defense.
key_cases.quote: a social worker must have a reasonable suspicion of child abuse before conducting an in-school interview when no other exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement applies

key_cases.case_name: A.P. v. Commonwealth, Cabinet for Health & Family Services
key_cases.holding: The court vacated a termination judgment because the family court conducted the first day of the termination trial, taking two witnesses' testimony, while the mother's appointed counsel was absent, holding that the mother was denied the due process to which she was entitled and ordering a new hearing with counsel present throughout.
key_cases.relevance: It illustrates how a voluntary safety plan created with a parent operates, and the consequences the Cabinet attaches to non-compliance.
key_cases.quote: Kentucky's statutory scheme to protect children and to adjudicate parental rights provides for the appointment of counsel throughout all the proceedings

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for a county social worker, holding that parents who voluntarily consented to a safety plan placing their children outside the home, and who never used the plan's stated mechanism for revoking that consent, were not entitled to any due-process hearing before or during the placement.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling Sixth Circuit rule that a genuinely voluntary safety plan requires no hearing, the first authority any Kentucky agency cites in defending a safety plan and the baseline Schulkers v. Kammer distinguishes on involuntariness.
key_cases.quote: the Smiths needed to explicitly withdraw the consent they explicitly gave, thus requiring Children's Services to either return the children or file a formal complaint against them
